topic: Physics — Forces and motion: Forces, accelerations and Newton's Laws of motion
subject: combined-science

items.q: A crate rests on a level floor. Its weight is 400 N downwards and the floor pushes upwards on it with a force of 400 N. Which statement about the crate is correct?
items.correct: The resultant force on the crate is zero, so it stays stationary.
items.misconception: No force at all acts on the crate while it is not moving.
items.why: Students read 'the resultant force is zero' as 'there is no force', because the two phrases describe the same visible outcome - an object that does not move. Zero resultant is not the same as no forces. Several forces can act and still add to nothing; remove the floor and the weight alone would show itself at once.
items.random_wrong: The crate's weight and the floor's push are a third law pair.

items.q: A puck slides in a straight line across a level ice rink at a steady 4 m/s. Friction and air resistance are so small that they can be ignored. What is the resultant force on the puck?
items.correct: It is zero, because the puck's velocity is not changing.
items.misconception: It acts forwards, because the puck is still moving forwards.
items.why: Everything that moves in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause. A resultant force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity indefinitely with no forward force at all.
items.random_wrong: It acts backwards, so the puck is very slowly stopping.

items.q: A van travels along a straight level road at a steady 25 m/s. The driving force from its engine is 900 N. What can be said about the resistive forces on the van?
items.correct: They total 900 N, acting backwards along the road.
items.misconception: They are smaller than 900 N, which is why the van moves.
items.why: Students associate a large driving force with fast motion rather than with acceleration, and think that staying in motion requires a surplus of force. A surplus of driving force would make the van speed up. A steady speed is the signature of balanced forces and a zero resultant.
items.random_wrong: They are larger than 900 N, so the van is losing speed.

items.q: A car is driven all the way round a roundabout at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Is there a resultant force acting on the car?
items.correct: Yes, because its direction is changing.
items.misconception: No, since the speed stays at a steady 10 m/s.
items.why: Speed and velocity are used interchangeably in everyday speech, so a fixed speedometer reading is taken to mean nothing about the motion is changing. Velocity includes direction. A change of direction alone is a change of velocity, and that requires a resultant force.
items.random_wrong: No, the forces on the car must all be balanced.

items.q: A skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity before opening her parachute. Which statement explains her motion?
items.correct: Her weight and the air resistance are equal, so the resultant is zero.
items.misconception: Her weight has fallen to zero, so nothing is pulling her downwards.
items.why: Students read 'the resultant force is zero' as 'there is no force', because the two phrases describe the same visible outcome - an object that does not move. Zero resultant is not the same as no forces. Several forces can act and still add to nothing; remove the floor and the weight alone would show itself at once.
items.random_wrong: The air resistance is now larger than her weight as she falls.

items.q: A book lies at rest on a table. Which statement about the forces on the book is correct?
items.correct: Its weight and the table's push give a resultant of zero.
items.misconception: There are no forces on the book while it lies still.
items.why: Students read 'the resultant force is zero' as 'there is no force', because the two phrases describe the same visible outcome - an object that does not move. Zero resultant is not the same as no forces. Several forces can act and still add to nothing; remove the floor and the weight alone would show itself at once.
items.random_wrong: The table's push must be bigger, to hold the book up.

items.q: (Higher tier) What is meant by the inertia of an object?
items.correct: Its tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.
items.misconception: A forward force that keeps a moving object going.
items.why: The word is used loosely outside physics, and describing motion as 'having momentum' or 'carrying force' makes inertia sound like a stored push. Inertia is a tendency, not a force. It appears in free body diagrams nowhere at all; what it describes is the absence of any need for a force to keep velocity constant.
items.random_wrong: A property that increases as an object moves faster.

items.q: (Higher tier) A bus brakes sharply and the standing passengers lurch forwards. Why does this happen?
items.correct: They keep moving at their original velocity.
items.misconception: A forward force throws them out of their places.
items.why: Everything that moves in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause. A resultant force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity indefinitely with no forward force at all.
items.random_wrong: Their inertia acts as a forward push on their bodies.

items.q: The resultant force acting on a trolley is doubled while its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration of the trolley?
items.correct: It doubles, as acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
items.misconception: Its speed doubles, but the acceleration stays as it was.
items.why: Everyday language links force to speed - pressing harder on the pedal 'makes it go faster' - and speed is easier to picture than rate of change of speed. Force sets the acceleration, not the speed. Twice the force means the velocity climbs twice as quickly, and the final speed depends on how long the force acts.
items.random_wrong: It halves, because the force has more work to do now.

items.q: The mass of a trolley is trebled while the resultant force acting on it is kept the same. What happens to its acceleration?
items.correct: The acceleration falls to a third of its old value.
items.misconception: It trebles, because the trolley is three times heavier.
items.why: Students expect the two quantities in a law to rise together, and heavy falling objects seem to 'go harder', so proportionality is applied where inverse proportionality is meant. In a = F / m the mass is on the bottom. Treble the mass under the same resultant force and the acceleration drops to one third.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, since the force is unchanged.

items.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a resultant force acting on it that gives it an acceleration of 2.5 m/s^2. What is the size of that resultant force?
items.why: The equation is recalled as a link between three quantities without its operation, so any arithmetic that uses both numbers looks defensible. resultant force = mass x acceleration is a multiplication. Check the answer with units: kg x m/s^2 gives N.

items.q: A go-kart and driver of total mass 500 kg have a driving force of 2500 N acting forwards on them and resistive forces of 500 N acting backwards. What is the acceleration?
items.why: The equation is remembered as 'force = mass x acceleration' without the word resultant, so the most prominent force in the question is substituted straight in. The F in F = m a is always the resultant. Combine all the forces first, then divide by the mass.

items.q: In the equation resultant force = mass x acceleration, which set of units must be used?
items.correct: force in newtons, N; mass in kilograms, kg; acceleration in m/s^2
items.misconception: force in newtons, N; mass in kilograms, kg; acceleration in m/s
items.why: Acceleration is described in words as a speed changing, and the squared second has no everyday meaning to attach it to. Acceleration is a change of velocity in m/s divided by a time in s, so its unit carries a second twice over: m/s^2.
items.random_wrong: force in newtons, N; mass in grams, g; acceleration in m/s^2

items.q: Why is acceleration measured in metres per second squared, m/s^2?
items.correct: A change of velocity in m/s is divided by a time in s.
items.misconception: A velocity in m/s is multiplied by the time taken.
items.why: 'Ratio' is remembered without its order, and either arrangement of the two quantities looks equally plausible on the page. Force over acceleration, matching m = F / a from F = m a. Check with units: N divided by m/s^2 gives kg.
items.random_wrong: A distance in metres is divided by a time in seconds twice.

items.q: (Higher tier) What does the inertial mass of an object measure?
items.correct: How difficult it is to change the object's velocity.
items.misconception: The size of the gravitational pull acting on the object.
items.why: Mass and weight are used as synonyms outside physics, and bathroom scales report a gravitational effect as though it were a mass. Inertial mass is about resisting a change of velocity, and it is measured in kilograms. It would be unchanged on the Moon, where the gravitational pull is not.
items.random_wrong: How fast the object is able to travel once it is released.

items.q: (Higher tier) How is inertial mass defined?
items.correct: As the ratio of force over acceleration.
items.misconception: As the acceleration divided by the force.
items.why: 'Ratio' is remembered without its order, and either arrangement of the two quantities looks equally plausible on the page. Force over acceleration, matching m = F / a from F = m a. Check with units: N divided by m/s^2 gives kg.
items.random_wrong: As the weight of the object divided by 10 N/kg.

items.q: A family car reaches a speed of about 27 m/s from rest in about 9 s. Estimate its acceleration.
items.correct: ~3 m/s^2, from a gain of about 27 m/s in about 9 s
items.misconception: ~27 m/s^2, the speed the car reaches on the road
items.why: In an estimation question the most prominent number is quoted back with the units of whatever is asked for, without the division being done. An estimate still needs the calculation. Divide the change of velocity by the time before rounding to a sensible one figure value.
items.random_wrong: ~240 m/s^2, from 27 m/s multiplied by the 9 s

items.q: A car of mass about 1000 kg accelerates at about 3 m/s^2. Estimate the resultant force acting on it.
items.correct: ~3000 N, from 1000 kg multiplied by 3 m/s^2
items.misconception: ~330 N, from 1000 kg divided by 3 m/s^2
items.why: The equation is recalled as a link between three quantities without its operation, so any arithmetic that uses both numbers looks defensible. resultant force = mass x acceleration is a multiplication. Check the answer with units: kg x m/s^2 gives N.
items.random_wrong: ~10 000 N, which is the weight of the car itself

items.q: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 3000 N' at the end of an estimate. What does the symbol ~ tell the reader?
items.correct: The 3000 N is an approximate value, not an exact one.
items.misconception: The force is smaller than 3000 N at every moment.
items.why: The symbol is confused with the inequality signs learned in mathematics, which do set an upper or a lower limit on a value. The symbol indicates an approximate value or approximate answer. The true value may lie either side of the figure quoted.
items.random_wrong: The force is at most 3000 N, never any higher.

items.q: In required practical activity 7, a trolley is pulled along a bench by masses hanging on a string over a pulley. When investigating how the force affects the acceleration, what must be kept constant?
items.correct: The total mass being accelerated.
items.misconception: The load left on the trolley.
items.why: The hanging masses are seen as the source of the force and the trolley as the object, so students forget that the hanging masses are accelerating too. The string accelerates the trolley and the hanging masses together. Transfer masses rather than adding them, so the total accelerating mass is constant.
items.random_wrong: The acceleration of the loaded trolley.

items.q: In the second part of required practical activity 7 the pulling force is kept constant and extra masses are placed on the trolley. What happens to the measured acceleration?
items.correct: It falls, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
items.misconception: It stays the same, as the pulling force has not changed.
items.why: Students latch onto the constant quantity named in the question and assume that whatever depends on it must also stay constant. Acceleration depends on both quantities. With F fixed, a = F / m falls as m rises, giving a curve rather than a horizontal line.
items.random_wrong: It rises, since a heavier trolley carries more force with it.

items.q: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with a force of 200 N. What force does the water exert on the swimmer?
items.correct: 200 N forwards, equal in size and opposite to her push.
items.misconception: Less than 200 N, because water is pushed aside so easily.
items.why: Students expect the sturdier or heavier object to win the exchange, and read 'equal and opposite' as applying only to evenly matched objects. The pair is always equal in size, whatever the two objects are. A fly striking a lorry pushes on it exactly as hard as the lorry pushes back.
items.random_wrong: 400 N forwards, twice as large as the swimmer's push.

items.q: A book rests in equilibrium on a table. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.correct: The book's push down on the table and the table's push up on it.
items.misconception: The weight of the book and the upward push of the table on the book.
items.why: Those two forces are equal and opposite in this situation, which is exactly the phrase used for a third law pair, so the label is attached to the wrong pair. A third law pair acts on two different objects and is the same kind of force. Weight and the table's push both act on the book, so they are balanced forces.
items.random_wrong: The weight of the book and the friction between it and the table.

items.q: A horse pulls a cart forwards. The cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why does the cart still accelerate?
items.correct: The two forces act on different objects.
items.misconception: Because the horse is far stronger than the cart is.
items.why: Students expect the sturdier or heavier object to win the exchange, and read 'equal and opposite' as applying only to evenly matched objects. The pair is always equal in size, whatever the two objects are. A fly striking a lorry pushes on it exactly as hard as the lorry pushes back.
items.random_wrong: It does not, so the loaded cart can never move.

items.q: An object moves at a constant velocity. Which way does the resultant force point?
items.correct: There is no resultant force, since the velocity is constant.
items.misconception: There must be a small backwards resultant force, because everything gradually slows down.
items.why: Real objects are slowed by friction and drag, so students carry that experience into questions that explicitly say those forces can be ignored. Read the question: if resistive forces are negligible or balanced, the resultant is zero and the speed does not fall at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two trolleys travel at the same speed, one heavy and one light. Which has more inertia?
items.correct: The heavier one, because inertia depends on mass, not on how fast the object is going.
items.misconception: The faster an object is travelling, the more inertia it has.
items.why: Fast objects are visibly harder to stop, so students tie the tendency to keep moving to the speed rather than to the mass. Inertia is the tendency to keep the state of motion, and it is measured by inertial mass. A stationary lorry has an enormous inertia while at rest.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 400 g trolley has a resultant force of 0.8 N on it. What is its acceleration?
items.correct: 2 m/s^2, after converting the mass to 0.4 kg.
items.misconception: 0.002 m/s^2, using the mass as 400 in the equation.
items.why: The number is given in grams and substituted without conversion, because the unit looks like a mass unit and the equation does not say which one to use. In F = m a the mass, m, is in kilograms, kg. Convert grams to kilograms before substituting, dividing by 1000.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the forces two objects exert on each other are equal and opposite, how can anything accelerate?
items.correct: The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel on either one.
items.misconception: They do cancel, so a horse can never actually get a cart moving.
items.why: Balanced forces and third law pairs both come as 'equal and opposite', and students add the two forces together as though they acted on one body. Only forces on the same object can be added. The cart accelerates because of the forces on the cart alone; the cart's pull acts on the horse.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A puck slides at 4 m/s with friction negligible. What is the resultant force on it?
items.correct: Zero, because the velocity of the puck is not changing.
items.misconception: A number given or just worked out can be written down as the answer even if it is a different quantity, such as a speed used as a force or a force used as an acceleration.
items.why: When no calculation seems possible, the only number in the question is reused with whatever unit the answer requires. A speed in m/s cannot become a force in N. Decide first whether the velocity is changing; if it is not, the resultant force is zero.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A book rests on a table. How does the table's upward push compare with the book's weight?
items.correct: They are equal in size, so the resultant force on the book is zero.
items.misconception: The table must push up harder than the weight pulls down, or the book would not be held up.
items.why: Holding something up feels like an effort, so students assume that supporting an object needs a surplus of upward force. A surplus upward force would accelerate the book upwards off the table. Holding it still needs the two forces to be equal, giving a zero resultant.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The resultant force on a trolley is doubled and its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration?
items.correct: It doubles, because acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
items.misconception: Nothing changes, because the mass of the trolley is the same as it was.
items.why: Half of the second law is remembered - that acceleration depends on mass - so a question that leaves the mass alone looks like a question with no change in it. Acceleration depends on both quantities: proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass. Change either one and the acceleration changes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In required practical 7, which quantity is the dependent variable?
items.correct: The acceleration of the trolley, which is measured for each force used.
items.misconception: The acceleration must be kept constant, because it is the quantity the experiment is about.
items.why: Control variables and the measured outcome are both described as things you 'look after' in a practical, so students hold the outcome fixed as well. The acceleration is what you measure and it must be free to change. Only the total accelerating mass is controlled in the first part of the practical.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water. Which way does the water's force on her act?
items.correct: Forwards, opposite to the direction of her push on the water.
items.misconception: Backwards, in the same direction as the force she applies.
items.why: Students match the size of the pair correctly but keep the direction of the original push, because the word 'equal' is remembered more firmly than the word 'opposite'. The forces two interacting objects exert on each other are equal AND opposite. If they acted the same way, no swimmer could ever move forwards.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can two forces that both act on the same object be a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.correct: No. A third law pair is one force on each of the two interacting objects.
items.misconception: Yes, as long as the two forces are equal in size they are a pair.
items.why: The test students remember is 'equal and opposite', which several pairs of forces in a diagram satisfy, so the object each force acts on is never checked. Identify the two objects first. One force of the pair acts on each of them; two forces drawn on one object can never be a third law pair.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
